title: First Commands to Teach a Puppy: 5 Cues to Start With
description: Which commands should you teach a puppy first? Step-by-step name, sit, down, come and leave it, with short sessions and rewards, backed by AKC and Dogs Trust.
excerpt: Name, sit, down, come and leave it: five first cues to teach your puppy, with simple steps and short, reward-based sessions.
seoTitle: First Commands to Teach a Puppy: 5 Cues to Start

html:
Start with your puppy's name, then sit, down, come and leave it. Use treats and praise, keep sessions to about five to ten minutes (AKC), and train in a safe, enclosed place. You can begin as soon as your puppy comes home, usually around 8 weeks old according to the AKC.

Before you start

  • Start early, keep it kind. AKC says puppies can begin very simple training as soon as they come home. Dogs Trust says the same.
  • Short sessions. AKC suggests five to ten minutes and ending on a positive note. RSPCA suggests short but regular sessions.
  • Rewards, not punishment. AKC says to avoid punishment such as leash corrections or yelling. RSPCA says all training should be reward based.
  • Go at your puppy's pace. Dogs Trust says what to work on depends on your puppy's needs and personality. RSPCA notes that dogs learn at different rates.
  • These are not the very first priority. AKC puts potty training, crate training and alone-time training first, with sit and down important but later. See our potty training schedule and crate training guide.
  • A puppy class helps. AKC suggests a positive-reinforcement puppy class once your vet says it is safe, and notes that until your puppy is fully vaccinated you should avoid unfamiliar dogs and potentially unclean environments. Talk to your vet first. See our puppy socialization checklist.

Rest matters (general guidance): a puppy who needs a nap will not learn well. See our nap and sleep schedule.

Why these five?

Sources do not agree on a single "first five." AKC's list is come, loose-leash walking, sit, down and stay. Dogs Trust's basics include name, sit, down, recall and leave it. We chose name, sit, down, come and leave it, because each has clear steps from at least one of these sources. Stay and loose-leash walking come next. Dogs Trust and AKC have separate guides for them.

1. Name (attention)

Dogs Trust says getting your dog to react to their name is essential for their safety.

  1. Start in a quiet room with small, high-value treats.
  2. Reward every time your puppy looks at you.
  3. Say the name. When your puppy looks, toss a treat to one side, then the other.
  4. Practice in busier places with extra treats.
  5. If your puppy ignores their name, do not keep repeating it. Move a little farther away and reward when they look. AKC also advises against repeating the name.

2. Sit

AKC, Dogs Trust and RSPCA all describe the same lure method.

  1. Hold a treat at your puppy's nose.
  2. Move it up and back over their head, so their bottom lowers.
  3. The moment they sit, mark it (say "yes" or click) and reward.
  4. Repeat without the treat in your hand.
  5. Add the word "sit" once your puppy sits reliably.

Do not push your puppy's bottom down (AKC, Dogs Trust).

3. Down

Teach this after sit (Dogs Trust, RSPCA).

  1. Start with your puppy sitting.
  2. Move a treat from their nose toward the floor between their paws.
  3. Mark and reward when they lie down.
  4. Repeat without the treat in your hand, then add the word "down" as they go down.
  5. If your puppy will not lie down, reward the first move toward the floor, then ask for a little more each time (Dogs Trust).

Never push your puppy's back down to force them (Dogs Trust).

4. Come (recall)

AKC says coming to you should be fun. Dogs Trust says to teach the name first.

  1. Practice indoors or in an enclosed area first. Say the name and your cue ("come" or "here"), step back, and reward when your puppy reaches you.
  2. Do not grab your puppy at the end (AKC).
  3. Add distance and distractions slowly. Outside, use a long line attached to a harness (Dogs Trust) in a safe, enclosed area (AKC).
  4. Only let your puppy off the lead in secure areas (Dogs Trust).
  5. Call sparingly. Give your puppy at least five seconds to respond before calling again (Dogs Trust).
  6. If your puppy does not come, stay calm. Getting angry or shouting will make them less likely to come back (Dogs Trust). Gently guide them in with the line, without pulling them toward you.

5. Leave it

Dogs Trust calls "leave" an incredibly helpful cue. It teaches this in two parts.

Part A: the fair trade. Offer a better treat for something your puppy has picked up, and reward them for giving it up. Add a cue such as "drop" once it works.

Part B: leave it. Hold a treat in one hand and a boring item in the other. Mark and reward your puppy for looking away, then add the cue "leave." Slowly add movement, distractions and better items.

If your puppy is mouthy, see our guide on how to stop puppy biting.

A simple way to fit it into the day

(General guidance) One or two five-minute sessions a day, with a potty trip first. Work on one cue at a time, and move on when your puppy is reliable in a quiet room. In your first week, our first week with a puppy guide helps you keep things manageable.

Troubleshooting

My puppy ignores me. Go back to a quieter place and better treats. Dogs Trust advises moving a little farther away and rewarding looks.

My puppy gets bored or silly. AKC says to slow down if a puppy struggles, and to end on a positive note.

My puppy will not come outside. Go back to the long line in a secure area. Do not chase.

Does it work for any breed? The sources say individual personality and learning speed matter. We did not find breed-specific timelines.

When to ask a professional

  • Your puppy seems fearful or shuts down in training
  • Biting, jumping or recall problems that are not improving
  • You want guidance on classes and your vet says it is not safe yet

Ask your vet and a qualified trainer. Dogs Trust has a behaviour support line for persistent problems. This article is general information, not veterinary advice.

quick: Start with your puppy's name, then sit, down, come and leave it. Use treats and praise, keep sessions to about five to ten minutes (AKC), and practice in a safe, enclosed place. You can begin as soon as your puppy comes home.

faq.q: What should I teach my puppy first?
faq.a: Many owners start with their name. AKC also puts potty, crate and alone-time training first.

faq.q: How long should training sessions be?
faq.a: AKC suggests five to ten minutes. RSPCA suggests short but regular sessions.

faq.q: At what age can I start?
faq.a: AKC says as soon as your puppy comes home, usually around 8 weeks old.
Yes. AKC describes positive reinforcement as the foundation of training.

faq.q: Can I punish my puppy for not listening?
faq.a: AKC and Dogs Trust advise against punishment and anger, especially for recall.

faq.q: Do I need a puppy class?
faq.a: AKC and RSPCA recommend classes. Ask your vet when it is safe, especially before your puppy is fully vaccinated.
